subject: Hierarchical modelling with PyStan (mixture of Gaussians  and Gaussian likelihood)

messages.author: 7a0d46cfe7d661bf
messages.subject: Hierarchical modelling with PyStan (mixture of Gaussians  and Gaussian likelihood)
parts:
This is the first time I use STAN (PyStan) and my first application on MCMC so I am trying to figure how to sample from the posterior distribution.
I want to fit a straight line to my data points with uncertainties in both the dependent and independent data points.
The equation of the line is:
                                             ytrue = alpha + beta * xtrue + epsilon
where epsilon ~ N(0, sigma), sigma is unknown and treated as a model parameter. 

My posterior distribution is 
                                          p(xtrue) * p(x | xtrue) * p(ytrue | alpha, beta, sigma, xtrue ) * p(ytrue | y)

My model is expressed hierarchically:

xtrue ~ mixture of Gaussians with weight: theta, mean: mu, and standard deviation: tau
ytrue ~ N(alpha + beta *xtrue, sigma)
x ~ N(xtrue, xerr) 
y ~ N(ytrue, yerr)

Here is my code:

data {

    int<lower=0> N; // number of points

    int<lower=0> K; // number of mixture gaussians

    vector[N] x; // x values

    vector[N] y; // y values

    real xerr; // x uncertainties

    real yerr; // y uncertainties

}


parameters {

    real alpha; // intercept

    real beta; // slope

    real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation ?! (check if s.d. or variance)

    vector[N] xtrue;

    vector[N] ytrue;

    simplex[K] theta;

    real mu[K];

    real<upper=0> tau[K];

}


model {

    vector[N] ymodel;

    real logxtrue[K];


    // PRIORS

    for (k in 1:K) {

    mu[k] ~ normal(0, 10);

    tau[k] ~ uniform(0, 100);

    }

    for (n in 1:N) {

        for (k in 1:K) {

             logxtrue[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(xtrue[n], mu[k], tau[k]);

         }

    lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(logxtrue);

    }


    ymodel <- alpha + beta * xtrue;

    ytrue ~ normal(ymodel, sigma);

    x ~ normal(xtrue, xerr);

    y ~ normal(ytrue, yerr);

}

"""




Question 1:
In STAN language, when I define x ~ normal(mean, sigma)
Is this the standard deviation or the variance? 

Question 2:
In my model I wrote the log distribution of xtrue but I wrote the usual normal distribution of ytrue, x, and y. Is this correct? How does STAN interpret normal(mean, sigma)? 
My concerns are that mathematically/statistically speaking I should either define my log-likelihood or my likelihood. In the model that I wrote above I used both of them, is this 'STAN-ically' correct?

Question 3:
Given the hierarchical model of my problem above, did I write my model correctly?

Question 4:
I ran the program but got the following error:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::normal_log: Scale parameter is -0.275754, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
Rejecting initialization at zero because of vanishing density.


Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts. 
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

Can someone please explain to me what is this error?

> Question 1:
> In STAN language, when I define x ~ normal(mean, sigma)
> Is this the standard deviation or the variance?

Variance --- the function part of the manual explains all the
formulas used for probability functions.

> Question 2:
> In my model I wrote the log distribution of xtrue but I wrote the usual normal distribution of ytrue, x, and y. Is this correct? How does STAN interpret normal(mean, sigma)?

y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

is, roughly speaking modulo constants, translated to

increment_log_prob(normal_log(y, mu, sigma));

The constants only affect efficiency and the value of lp__ up to a constant.

> My concerns are that mathematically/statistically speaking I should either define my log-likelihood or my likelihood. In the model that I wrote above I used both of them, is this 'STAN-ically' correct?

It's always a log density including both log prior and log likelihood
if you've decomposed your density that way.

> Question 3:
> Given the hierarchical model of my problem above, did I write my model correctly?

No.

First, that's not a hierarchical model in the statistical sense.
It's a mixture model.

But it's not right for a mixture model because of this:

> real<upper=0> tau[K];
> tau[k] ~ uniform(0, 100);

Every parameter should have support for every value matching its
declared constraints. Here the constraint is upper=0, which admits
values of -10, which are out of support. We don't recommend these
flat bounded priors anyway --- see the regression chapter of the manual
for our current thinking on priors.

But you don't want just lower=0, either. You either want to
change the prior to not be on a constrained interval (recommended)
or change the constraint to <lower=0, upper=100> to match the support
in the model.

> Question 4:
> I ran the program but got the following error:
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::normal_log: Scale parameter is -0.275754, but must be > 0!
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
> Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
> Rejecting initialization at zero because of vanishing density.
>
>
> Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
> Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
>
> Can someone please explain to me what is this error?

Yes, you have a scale parameter that's negative but it has
to be positive.

You have this:

> real<upper=0> tau[K];

where you needed <lower=0,upper=100> given that (a) you need it to
be positive, and (b) you needed it to be constrained to (0,100) for
the uniform(0,100).

- Bob

Sorry --- not so much misremembering as answering e-mail
too fast. Definitely standard deviation so that it's on
the same scale as the data.
> Also, one more thing. If you’re fitting a mixture model you need some constraint to identify which mixture component is which.

Section 19.2 (Label Switching in Mixture Models) covers what I know
about the problem. There's a subsection "Hacks as Fixes" that covers
some of the options, such as ordering parameters.

I know Andrew's been thinking about this more lately in the multivariate
setting.

- Bob
